items.title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’
items.summary:
There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world

The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles.

Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. The schnitzel has to be pounded until paper-thin, the breadcrumb coating must be light and airy, the accompanying potato salad prepared with a marinade of beef stock, vinegar, oil and finely chopped onions – without (without!) mayonnaise. Anything else is an affront. In Vienna you can get heated debates with strangers about all sorts of ideological nonsense. But the quality of a schnitzel is not up for discussion. The Viennese take food seriously, but without coming across as particularly serious. If you’ve nothing to laugh about at the dinner table, you’ve…

items.title: Vienna on a plate: a food lover’s guide to the Austrian capital
items.summary:
Some of the city’s best chefs, Ola Szwarc, Nadim Amin, Konstantin Filippou and Felix Mandl, share their favourite cafes, bars and restaurants

There are two sides to coffee in Vienna. The grand, old-school coffee houses are incredible places to sit, have breakfast, drink a beer and forget about time. They have much the same function as a pub in Britain. For that experience, we’d go to Café Prückel or Café Hawelka. For a quintessential Viennese coffee, we’d suggest a wiener melange – somewhat similar to a cappuccino, but traditionally a little milder, made with coffee, steamed milk and milk foam. Alternatively, an einspänner is another peculiar, old-fashioned option: a strong black coffee served in a glass with a layer of cold whipped cream on top. If we want good coffee that actually wakes us up, we go to Kaffeemodul. You can choose the style you like, from fruity to less fruity. NA

items.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for almond sorbet with grape granita
items.summary:
This dessert makes me feel like I’m in Sicily again

Ice-cream holds an irresistible allure for me. That combination of richness, lightness, and the pure, sensual pleasure of it melting gently across the palate maintains an unbreakable hold over my imagination. In fact, other than fruit, it’s the only sweet food with which I have a genuine emotional relationship: I can remember many ice-creams I’ve eaten incredibly vividly, and in a way I just don’t with almost all other desserts and pastries. Today’s ice is a case in point, having been developed from a memory of an almond gelato eaten in Sicily just after the annual harvest.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

This story was previously published as part of that series. Subscribe to Eater Today to see more of our editors’ boldest opinions about dining culture writ large. 

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well. 

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task ( “Nobody wants to make puff pastry!” ). 

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s…

As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary:
Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce

Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan, whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat.

The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. Hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, abandoned parks and wastelands are all places in which you might find yourself close to a plum tree; its branches decorated with fruit, some the size of marbles, others lozenges or eggs, and their spectrum of colour ranging from deep purple to powdery light blue, red, pink, gold and green.

And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. items.title: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert
items.summary:
The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Consider this your cheat sheet for next time you’re asked to bring something tasty to the party | Eater Staff 

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests. 

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options. 

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.
